title: Quantum PCP: a constant promise gap for local Hamiltonians
formal: Are there constants $k$ and $\varepsilon>0$ for which the following promise problem is QMA-hard? The input is $H=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m H_i$ on $n$ qubits, with each term acting on at most $k$ qubits and $0\preceq H_i\preceq I$. Distinguish $\lambda_{\min}(H)\le a$ from $\lambda_{\min}(H)\ge b$, promised $b-a\ge\varepsilon$. The reduction must be efficient. This is the normalized Hamiltonian formulation.
why: This asks whether approximating a quantum system’s energy captures the full difficulty of quantum witness verification. It connects complexity, quantum codes, and local testing.

title: Strong quantum IOPs with polynomial communication
formal: Does every QMA promise problem admit a constant-round strong quantum interactive oracle proof with a uniform polynomial-time verifier, total prover-message length polynomial in the input length n, total query complexity O(1), completeness at least 2/3, and soundness at most 1/3? The strong access model is defined below. The prover may be computationally unbounded, and soundness quantifies over all prover strategies.
why: The problem isolates the communication price of an extremely limited quantum verifier. A positive result would eliminate the exponential communication in the present strong construction.

title: Does a quantum witness have more power than a classical witness?
formal: Is $\mathrm{QMA}=\mathrm{QCMA}$? Both classes have a polynomial-time quantum verifier and bounded error. QMA permits a polynomial-size quantum witness; QCMA permits only a polynomial-length classical string. The question concerns the standard classes without an oracle.
why: This identifies what kind of information might be intrinsically necessary for efficient verification.

title: Quantum versus classical nonuniform advice
formal: Is $\mathrm{BQP/qpoly}=\mathrm{BQP/poly}$? Advice for inputs of length $n$ depends only on $n$: a state on $\operatorname{poly}(n)$ qubits on the left, or $\operatorname{poly}(n)$ classical bits on the right. The computation must succeed on every input of that length.
why: This distinguishes two basic ways to store auxiliary information for computation. It is different from QMA versus QCMA.
